slides.title: LIKE search: fine on small data, breaks on big data
slides.tldr: LIKE %x% reads every row, ignores typos, and has no idea which result fits best.

blocks.title: Opening every book in the library
blocks.body: A library holds 500,000 books. You ask, "Give me every book that mentions pasta." If the librarian flips through every page of every book, it will be evening before you get an answer. `LIKE '%pasta%'` does exactly that: it reads every row in the table to see whether the word appears anywhere in the text. An ordinary index doesn't help, because it is sorted like a dictionary, by the **first letters**.

blocks.code:
-- a table of 500,000 products
SELECT id, name FROM product
WHERE name LIKE '%phone%' OR description LIKE '%phone%'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- EXPLAIN says: type = ALL, rows ≈ 500000
-- i.e. no index was used, the whole table was read

marks.tip: The leading % makes the B-tree index useless, so the database reads the full text of every row to compare.
You get the newest product first, not the best match. SQL has no idea which result is more relevant.

blocks.caption: What the customer typed, what LIKE did, and what the customer really wanted

rows.tip: In the name, "samsung" and "phone" are not next to each other ("Galaxy A15" sits between them), so the exact fragment never matched.
LIKE doesn't know that phones and phone are two forms of the same word. It only compares characters.
A one-letter typo. A person understands it at once; LIKE does not.
As long as the characters match, LIKE is happy. It has no judgment about what to show first.

aside.body: While you have a few thousand products, a search box built on LIKE works fine. The trouble shows up later: the page takes seconds to open, and customers say "I can't find anything."

items.meaning: Reading every row of a table because no index can be used.
A measure of how well a result fits what was searched for.

check.q: The name column has an index. Why is LIKE '%phone%' still slow while LIKE 'phone%' is fast?
check.a: An index is sorted by the start of the text. If the start is known, the database can jump straight there; with a leading %, it has no idea where to begin, so it reads every row.

slides.title: Inverted index: from a word to its documents
slides.tldr: An inverted index lists, for every word, the documents that contain it; searching is just fetching that list.

blocks.title: The index at the back of a book
blocks.body: A thick book has an index at the back: "pasta: pages 12, 87, 203". To find the word you don't read the whole book, you look at one line. Now imagine the librarian building one such notebook for the entire library, with every word followed by the books it appears in. That notebook is an **inverted index**. A table says "book → words"; this notebook runs the other way and says "word → books".

blocks.caption: An inverted index built from three product names

rows.tip: The word appears in document 1 (Samsung Galaxy phone) and 3 (Samsung charger). This list is called a posting list.
It appears in document 1 (Samsung Galaxy phone) and 2 (Phone cover).
Only in document 1. A word that appears in few places is worth more when searching.
Only in document 2 (Phone cover).
Only in document 3 (Samsung charger).

blocks.caption: What happens inside the index when you search "samsung phone"

nodes.label: Search
nodes.tip: What the customer typed. It is first split into separate words.

nodes.label: samsung
nodes.tip: The posting list for samsung is pulled straight from the notebook, with no document read at all.

nodes.label: phone
nodes.tip: The posting list for phone is pulled out the same way.

nodes.label: Combine
nodes.tip: Combining two short sorted lists is very cheap. Even with millions of documents it takes milliseconds.

nodes.label: Result
nodes.tip: Document 1 contains both words, so it goes to the top. Documents 2 and 3 each match one word.

edges.label: The search is split into words; the list for samsung is fetched
The list for phone is fetched too
samsung appears in documents 1 and 3
phone appears in documents 1 and 2
Both lists contain 1, so it comes first

blocks.body: To do less work at search time, do more work at write time. An index is work done in advance.

items.meaning: One item stored in a search engine, such as a product. Like a row in a table.
A single word stored in the index.
The sorted list of documents in which a term appears.

aside.body: A table goes document → words. An inverted index goes word → documents. Flip the direction and searching gets easy.

check.q: In the index above, which document comes first for "samsung charger", and why?
check.a: Document 3. The list for samsung is (1, 3) and the list for charger is (3), and only 3 appears in both.

slides.title: Analyzer: the factory that turns text into terms
slides.tldr: An analyzer splits text into words, lowercases them and reduces them to their root; if index and query don't use the same analyzer, words won't match.

blocks.body: If "Phones", "phone" and "PHONE" went into the notebook as three separate lines, searching for "phone" would miss the other two. So before anything is written down, every piece of text passes through a small factory called an **analyzer**. Inside it, a **tokenizer** cuts the text into words and **token filters** bring those words to a common form. The customer's search text goes through the same factory.

blocks.caption: How "Samsung Phones for Gaming" becomes three terms

steps.title: 1. Character filter
steps.body: Strips HTML tags: Samsung Phones for Gaming
steps.tip: A cleanup before the text is cut. html_strip removes tags; other filters can swap characters.

steps.title: 2. Tokenizer
steps.body: Cuts into words: Samsung · Phones · for · Gaming
steps.tip: The standard tokenizer cuts at spaces and punctuation. Each piece is called a token.

steps.title: 3. Lowercase
steps.tip: From now on Samsung, SAMSUNG and samsung are one and the same term.

steps.title: 4. Stop words
steps.body: Drops filler words: samsung · phones · gaming
steps.tip: Words like for, the and is appear in almost every text, so they are useless for searching.

steps.title: 5. Stemmer
steps.body: Reduces to the root: samsung · phone · game
steps.tip: phones → phone, gaming → game. Now searching "phone" finds this product too. The root isn't always a real word, and that's fine.

marks.tip: The real index is called products_v1, and the app always says products. That nickname (an alias) lets you swap in a rebuilt index later without touching any code.
The filters run in exactly this order. Without lowercase first, the stop word filter and the stemmer won't recognize capitalized words.
text means the analyzer runs, for searching inside the full text. product_text is used at both index time and query time.
keyword means no analyzer: the whole value is one exact term. This is what you need for filters, sorting and facets.

blocks.body: Same analyzer on both sides, index and query. Otherwise the word sits in the notebook and never matches.

items.desc: Send an analyzer and some text in the body to see which terms it produces

items: Elasticsearch ships ready-made language analyzers such as `english` and `spanish`. If names mix English and Spanish, keep two fields with two analyzers.
A synonym filter can make "mobile" and "phone" the same. Teach the engine the words your customers actually use.

items.meaning: A piece cut by the tokenizer; once it passes the filters and lands in the index, it is a term.
Trimming the end of a word to get its root (phones → phone).

check.q: Product names were indexed with a lowercase filter, but the search text skips it. What happens when you search "Samsung"?
check.a: Nothing matches. The notebook holds "samsung" and you are looking for "Samsung", and to the search engine those are two different terms.

slides.title: Relevance: which result comes first
slides.tldr: A search engine gives every document a score (BM25): higher for rare words, for repeated words, and for matches in short text.

blocks.body: The librarian searches "pasta recipe" and finds 300 books. Handing them all over in a heap doesn't help; the most useful book must be on top. So the search engine gives every document a number called its **score** and shows the highest first. Elasticsearch calculates it with a formula called BM25, which looks at three things.

blocks.title: The three things BM25 looks at
items: **How rare the word is:** "recipe" is in a thousand books, "pasta" in only 40. Matching a rare word scores higher.
**How often it appears:** more occurrences raise the score, but only up to a limit.
**How short the text is:** "pasta" in a five-word title is not the same as "pasta" in the corner of a 500-page book.

blocks.caption: Scores of three products for the search "samsung phone" (example)

items.label: Samsung Galaxy Phone
items.tip: Both words match, and inside a short name, so this gets the highest score.

items.label: Samsung Charger
items.tip: Only samsung matched. The word is fairly rare, so the score is middling.

items.label: Phone Cover
items.tip: Only phone matched, and phone appears in thousands of products, so the score is low.

marks.tip: name^3 gives a match in the name three times the weight of a match in the description. This is called a boost.
Tolerates a typo of one or two letters, so even "samsang" brings back Samsung products.

blocks.body: Search is not just "is it there?" but "how well does it fit?"

items.meaning: How many times the word appears in one document.
How rare the word is across the whole index; the rarer, the more it is worth.
Manually giving a field or condition extra weight.

items: Add `"explain": true` to the query and every result shows exactly how its score was calculated.
Business signals such as sales or ratings can be blended into the score (`function_score`), but fix names and analyzers first.

check.q: Searching "pasta recipe", which book scores higher: one with "pasta" in its title, or one with "recipe" in a corner of its 500 pages? Why?
check.a: The one with "pasta" in the title. "Pasta" is a rare word and it matched in very short text, and both of those raise the score.

slides.title: Searching from Symfony: results and facets in one request
slides.tldr: A facet is a counted list like "Samsung (12), Apple (8)" beside the results; send the query, filter and aggregation in one request.

blocks.body: Type "phone" in an online shop and the left side shows: Samsung (12), Apple (8). That counted list is a **facet**. It splits the results into groups and shows how many fall in each, so the customer can narrow the list with one click. Elasticsearch calls it an aggregation. The search text goes in `must`, where it gets a score. A plain yes-or-no condition such as "in stock" goes in `filter`. The brand the customer clicks goes in `post_filter`, which trims the hits only after the counting is done. Put it in the main query instead, and the facet shrinks to Samsung (12) alone, with no way to switch brands.

blocks.code:
framework:
    http_client:
        scoped_clients:
            search.client:
                base_uri: '%env(SEARCH_URL)%'

marks.tip: The scoped client named search.client is autowired automatically into an argument called $searchClient.
The query inside must calculates scores, so this is where the order of products is decided.
A filter never changes the score; it only excludes, and Elasticsearch caches the result. Yes/no conditions belong here. in_stock is a boolean field in the mapping.
Counts the products matched per brand, before post_filter runs: [{key: samsung, doc_count: 12}, {key: apple, doc_count: 8}]. The field must be a keyword.
Runs after the counting. The hits shrink to Samsung, but the facet still lists Apple (8). The price: post_filter is not cached and speeds nothing up, so use it only for the facet's own field.

blocks.caption: Results and facets in one request

nodes.label: Vue app
nodes.tip: The customer types and clicks facets here. Instead of a request per keystroke, send one 300ms after typing stops.

nodes.label: ProductSearch
nodes.tip: Builds the Elasticsearch query from what the customer typed and picked. The browser never talks to Elasticsearch directly.

nodes.label: Elasticsearch
nodes.tip: Finds the matching documents in the inverted index, scores them, and counts them by brand in the same pass.

edges.label: The customer types "phone" and picks the brand Samsung
The query, filter, aggs and post_filter go in one request
20 Samsung hits ranked by score come back, plus counts for every brand
Vue shows the facets on the left and the results on the right

items: Running an aggregation on a `text` field throws an error. Always keep facet fields as `keyword`.
`post_filter` is only for the facet's own field. Every other condition (in stock, a price range) belongs in `filter`, so it is cached and the counts shrink with it.
Never expose Elasticsearch directly to the internet; every request should go through Symfony.

items.meaning: Splitting the results into groups and counting the documents in each group.
One group of an aggregation, such as brand = samsung, together with its count.

check.q: A customer types "phone" and picks Samsung, yet should still see Apple (8) listed. Where do the text, the brand and "in stock" go?
check.a: "phone" goes in must, because it needs a score. The brand goes in post_filter, so the counts are made before it trims the hits. "In stock" goes in filter: yes or no, no score, cached.

slides.title: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: when to bring one in, when not to
slides.tldr: A search engine is powerful, but you must run a separate cluster, keep data in sync and accept a delay of a second or two; for small data, database full-text is enough.

blocks.body: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch are both search engines built on the same library, Lucene, so the inner concepts and the API are almost identical. (OpenSearch is an Apache 2.0 fork of Elasticsearch 7.10.) Both give excellent search, but not for free: it is one more moving part in your system, which you have to run, monitor and keep in sync with the database. The cheapest path is already in your database, so it is shown first, below the comparison.

blocks.caption: Three paths: what you get and what you pay

columns.title: Database full-text
items: No new server needed
Data is always fresh, inside the transaction
Often enough up to a few hundred thousand rows
Weak at typos, facets and fine-grained ranking
columns.tip: A tsvector column with a GIN index in PostgreSQL, a FULLTEXT index in MySQL. Under the hood this is an inverted index too.

columns.title: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
items: Typos, synonyms, facets, language analyzers
Answers in milliseconds even on tens of millions of documents
A separate cluster: RAM, monitoring, upgrades, backups
Must be synced from the database; lags by a second or two
Changing an analyzer or mapping means a full reindex
columns.tip: A full search engine. It does the most, and costs the most to run.

columns.title: Meilisearch / Typesense
items: Easy to run and learn
Great for small to medium catalogs
Limited on huge data or complex aggregations
Also needs syncing from the database
columns.tip: Small, simple search engines. Easy to set up, and they handle typos out of the box.

blocks.file: PostgreSQL: the database route, in full

marks.tip: Weight A for the name, B for the description: a match in the name ranks higher, like the name^3 boost in Elasticsearch.
STORED means the database fills this column on every insert and update, inside the same transaction, so it is never stale. Needs PostgreSQL 12 or newer.
GIN is an inverted index: the same word to rows list as before. Without it, every search reads the whole table again, exactly like LIKE.
The english configuration lowercases and stems, so "phones" becomes phone and matches. websearch_to_tsquery accepts text as typed in a search box and never errors.
ts_rank counts matches and weights, nothing more. It is simpler than BM25 and does not know that a word is rare. A typo like "samsang" still finds nothing.

blocks.title: The decision rule
items: Start with database full-text.
Bring in a search engine when real complaints arrive about typos, facets, language or ranking.
Whatever you keep in the search engine must be rebuildable from the database on any day.

blocks.body: A search index is a copy, not the source of truth. Never base a decision about money or stock on the index.

items: Doctrine doesn't know the `search_vector` column, so the next `make:migration` may propose dropping it. Read every generated migration before you run it.
PostgreSQL ships no Japanese configuration. For Japanese text use `simple` (no stemming), or move to an engine that has a Japanese analyzer.

use: Searching is the customer's main task: an e-commerce catalog, job listings, documents.
You need typo tolerance, facets and text that mixes Japanese and English.
avoid: A short list in an admin panel, searched by name or ID.
Nobody on the team can run a cluster, and there is no budget for a managed service.

items.label: Keeping the search index up to date
The real cost of new technology

check.q: Ryan's shop has 8,000 products, one server and a team of two. What should he choose for search first, and why?
check.a: Database full-text search (a tsvector column with a GIN index). At that size it is fast enough, with no new server and no sync. Move to a search engine when complaints arrive.

slides.title: In the database, missing from search
slides.tldr: Write to the database and the search index separately from a controller and one failure leaves them disagreeing; this trap is called a dual write.

blocks.body: Right after saving a product, Ryan's controller writes straight to Elasticsearch. In library terms: putting the book on the shelf and writing its name in the catalog notebook are two jobs in two places. One day Elasticsearch was down for half a minute. In that gap, 40 products landed in the database but never reached the index. Sellers phone in: "I listed my product and I can't find it." This trap of writing to two places separately is called a **dual write**.

marks.tip: Committed right here. Whatever happens next, the product stays in the database.
If this request fails, or the process dies halfway, the product never reaches the index, and nobody retries it later.
The customer waits until Elasticsearch answers. If search is slow, saving a product is slow too.

blocks.caption: One request, two writes, and the second one fails

actors.label: Controller
actors.tip: It has taken on the job of writing to both places itself.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: The source of truth lives here. Its commit can't be taken back.

actors.label: Elasticsearch
actors.tip: The search index: a copy of the database, running on a separate server.

messages.tip: The customer thinks the product wasn't saved and tries again, so the database now holds the same product twice.
This mismatch between the two places will never heal on its own.

aside.body: You can't write "both or neither" across two separate systems. So one of them must be the source of truth, and the other must follow behind it.

items.meaning: Writing the same data to two separate systems independently; if one fails, they disagree.
The mismatch that builds up between a copy and its source over time.

check.q: If the Elasticsearch request fails after flush() succeeds, what state are the database and the index left in?
check.a: The product is in the database but not in the index. The database commit can't be undone and nobody retries the index write, so the mismatch stays.

slides.title: The database is the original, the index is its copy, with a pipeline in between
slides.tldr: Write to the database first, then put a message with just the ID on a queue; a worker reads the fresh state from the database and updates the index.

blocks.title: The books on the shelf and the catalog notebook
blocks.body: In a library, the books on the shelves are the original and the catalog notebook is the copy. When a new book arrives, the librarian puts it on the shelf and drops a slip into a basket: "Book 42 changed." Later an assistant picks up the slip, **goes to the shelf and looks at the book himself**, and only then updates the notebook. The slip carries no description of the book, just the number. So even if a slip arrives twice, or out of order, the notebook still gets the shelf's latest state.

blocks.caption: The pipeline from the database to the search index

nodes.label: API
nodes.tip: The librarian. It writes only to the database and sends one small message; it never talks to Elasticsearch.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: The books on the shelf. Every write happens here first, and every final answer comes from here.

nodes.label: Queue
nodes.tip: The basket of slips. Even if Elasticsearch is down, the message waits here safely.

nodes.label: Worker
nodes.tip: The assistant. It picks up a message, re-reads the product from the database, then writes to the index. If that fails, it tries again.

nodes.label: Search index
nodes.tip: The catalog notebook. If it is lost, the whole thing can be rebuilt from the database.

edges.label: The database is written first: this is the source of truth
Then just a "product 42 changed" message goes on the queue
The worker picks the message up in its own time
It reads the latest state of product 42 from the database
It overwrites the index document with that state

blocks.title: This design removes three dangers
items: Elasticsearch down? The message waits in the queue and the worker retries later.
The same message arrives twice? The same document is written again, and no harm is done.
Messages arrive out of order? The worker always reads the database's latest state anyway.

blocks.body: Put an ID in the message, not the data. Before writing, the worker always reads fresh state from the database.

items.meaning: The place whose data counts as final; everything else is a copy.
A copy built from the original data that can be deleted and rebuilt: a search index, a cache, a report.

items: Bigger systems skip the message and read the database's change log to update the index (CDC). The principle is the same: database first, index behind it.

check.q: If the message carries only the ID instead of the product's new price, which two problems go away on their own?
check.a: The same message arriving twice and messages arriving out of order. Either way the worker reads the latest state from the database, so an old price can't reach the index.

slides.title: The write side: flush, then one small message
slides.tldr: The write code only flushes to the database and dispatches an IndexProduct message; the message goes to its own transport, with retries.

blocks.body: The write code now has just two jobs: flush to the database, then send a small message through Symfony Messenger. It doesn't even know Elasticsearch exists. The message goes to its own transport, which is a lane of its own, so search work can't hold up the lane that carries emails or payment messages.

marks.tip: The message holds only the ID: no name, no price. That way a message can never go stale.
Don't send the message until the database has committed; otherwise the worker will read the old state.
dispatch just writes one row to a queue, a few milliseconds of work. The customer never waits for Elasticsearch.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        failure_transport: failed
        transports:
            search_index:
                dsn: 'doctrine://default?queue_name=search_index'
                retry_strategy:
                    max_retries: 5
                    delay: 2000      # first retry after 2 seconds
                    multiplier: 3    # then 6, 18, 54, 162 seconds (about 4 minutes in all)
            failed: 'doctrine://default?queue_name=failed'
        routing:
            App\Message\IndexProduct: search_index

marks.tip: A separate queue. If you switch to RabbitMQ or Redis, only this dsn changes and the rest of the code stays the same.
If it still fails after five tries (about 4 minutes in all), the message is parked in the failed transport. It isn't lost, and you can rerun it by hand later.

blocks.title: One gap is still open: a crash between flush and dispatch
items: If the process dies between `flush()` and `dispatch()`, the product is saved but no message exists, so nothing will ever index it.

Cheap cure: a nightly job re-sends IndexProduct for everything changed in the last 24 hours (safe, the handler is idempotent). Price: a lost message waits up to a day, and hard-deleted rows are missed.
Strong cure: the outbox. Save the message in the same transaction as the product, and a relay sends it. Price: an extra table and a relay process.

items.desc: How many messages are waiting in each queue

check.q: What could go wrong if you dispatch the IndexProduct message before flush()?
check.a: The worker might pick up the message before the commit and read the database too early. It would get the old state and write that to the index. So the order is always: flush first, dispatch after.

slides.title: The read side: a handler that is safe to run again and again
slides.tldr: The handler reads the product from the database: PUT it under its own ID if it exists, DELETE if not, and throw on failure so Messenger retries.

blocks.body: The assistant's job must work in such a way that even if the same slip arrives ten times, the notebook stays correct. This property is called being **idempotent**: doing it once or many times gives the same result. The trick is simple: use the product's ID as the document's ID, and `PUT` to replace the whole document. A second write then creates nothing new; it just puts the same document in place again.

marks.tip: Whatever the message says, the truth is always re-read from the database.
Product deleted or hidden? Then remove it from the index too. No separate message is needed for deletes.
404 means it was already gone, which counts as success. Anything else throws, so Messenger retries.
A PUT with an ID replaces the whole document. Run it ten times and the index still holds one document. toSearchDocument() also feeds the rebuild, so both always agree.
getContent() throws on a 4xx/5xx or a failed connection, and that one line is what switches retries on.

blocks.caption: What the handler does in four situations

rows.tip: A new product creates the document and an existing one replaces it, with the very same request.
If the document is already gone you get a 404, which is treated as success.
A queue delivers a message at least once, and sometimes twice. Because the handler is idempotent, that is fine.
Per retry_strategy it tries again after 2, 6, 18... seconds, and finally parks the message in the failed transport.

aside.body: Same ID, PUT the whole thing, read the truth from the database: these three make a handler idempotent.

items: A `POST /products/_doc` without an ID creates a new document every time, so the same product shows up twice in search.
If two workers write the same product at once, the older state can land last. Adding `?version=…&version_type=external` makes Elasticsearch reject the older one.

items.label: Why a message can arrive twice

check.q: If the same IndexProduct message reaches the handler three times, how many documents end up in the index, and why?
check.a: Just one. The product ID is the document ID, and each PUT replaces that same document in full, so nothing new is created.

slides.title: The gap of a few seconds: eventual consistency
slides.tldr: There will always be a gap of a second or two between a database write and its appearing in search; serve the page right after a write, and every decision, from the database.

blocks.body: Between a slip landing in the basket and the notebook being updated, a little time passes. During that time the shelf and the notebook tell different stories, and then they agree again on their own. This is called **eventual consistency**. The gap comes from three places: waiting in the queue, the worker's own work, and Elasticsearch itself, which only makes new writes searchable once every second. This isn't a bug. It is the price of this design.

blocks.caption: A seller lists a product and immediately searches for it

actors.label: Seller
actors.tip: Lists a product and wants to see at once whether it is up.

actors.label: API
actors.tip: It has written to the database and sent the message; its job is done.

actors.label: Search index
actors.tip: The worker hasn't written here yet, so it knows nothing so far.

messages.label: Not found
messages.tip: The product is in the database, but the index is still a second or two behind.

blocks.title: Four rules for living with the gap
items: Show the page right after a write from the database, such as "My products" or the edit page.
Decide about money, stock and permissions from the database; search is only for finding things.
Tell users: "It may take a few seconds to show up in search."
Measure the gap: how many messages are waiting in the queue, and how old the oldest one is.

blocks.body: A copy always runs a little behind. Design by accepting that, not by denying it.

items.meaning: Once writes stop, all copies end up in the same state eventually, though not instantly.
How often Elasticsearch makes new writes searchable; usually 1 second.

items: Adding `?refresh=true` to every write shrinks the gap, but indexing becomes much slower. Don't use it outside tests.
Don't put `sleep(2)` in a controller to hide the gap; on a busy day the gap will exceed 2 seconds, and every request is slowed for nothing.

items.label: Consistency models: who sees what, and when

check.q: A seller saves a product but doesn't see it on the "My products" page. Where should that page read its data from to avoid the problem?
check.a: From the database. A page shown right after a write that reads from the search index exposes the gap to the user; reading from the database lets them see their own write at once.

slides.title: Rebuilding the whole index with zero downtime
slides.tldr: Build a new index and fill it from the database in batches, then flip an alias in one step; the app always knows the alias, never the real index.

blocks.body: When the analyzer or mapping changes, you can't patch the old catalog notebook; you have to start a new one and copy every book from the shelves again. To keep readers from noticing, they always look at "the notebook on the table", and they never know which notebook is actually there. In Elasticsearch this table is called an **alias**: a nickname that points at a real index.

blocks.caption: Moving the products alias from v1 to v2

steps.title: 1. Create the new index
steps.body: products_v2 with the new mapping. The app still reads v1 through the alias.
steps.tip: The old index isn't touched, so search works normally the whole time.

steps.title: 2. Stop the worker
steps.body: Stop the search_index worker; new messages pile up in the queue.
steps.tip: This way no write is lost and no old state overwrites a new one while filling. The cost: search is a little stale for these few minutes.

steps.title: 3. Fill from the database
steps.body: Load every product into v2, 500 at a time, with _bulk.
steps.tip: One by one, 2 million products means 2 million requests. At 500 per bulk it is 4,000 requests.

steps.title: 4. Verify
steps.body: Compare the database count with v2 and run a few familiar searches.
steps.tip: This is the last chance before the flip. If you find a mistake, delete v2 and start over, and no customer will have noticed.

steps.title: 5. Flip the alias
steps.body: In one atomic step, products → v2.
steps.tip: The very next search request uses the new index. There is no moment in between when the alias is empty.

steps.title: 6. Start the worker
steps.body: Queued messages now go to v2. Delete v1 a few days later.
steps.tip: The worker reads fresh state from the database, so replaying the queued messages brings v2 up to date. While v1 exists, a rollback is just flipping the alias back.

marks.tip: toIterable() fetches one row at a time; even a million products never sit in memory together.
Each bulk document takes two lines: first what to do (index, with the ID), then the document itself.
Clear Doctrine's memory after every batch, or a long job will run out of memory.
The bulk request itself returns 200 even when some documents fail, so you must check the errors field of the response.
Every action in the list happens together or not at all, so no search request ever finds an empty alias.

blocks.body: The app never knows the real index name, only the alias.

use: An analyzer or a field type has changed.
The index has drifted from the database, or the cluster itself was lost.
avoid: You only added a new field: add it to the existing mapping and reindex the products.

items: If filling takes hours, don't stop the worker; have the handler write to both indexes and use external versions.

check.q: What would be the problem in moving to a new index if the app's code had products_v1 written into it directly?
check.a: Changing the name would need a code deploy, and during the deploy some servers would read the old index and some the new one. With an alias, everyone switches to the new index together in one request.

slides.title: The same calculation, 50,000 times a day
slides.tldr: Recomputing an answer that barely changes on every request wastes time and servers; a cache keeps that answer on hand.

blocks.title: The counter at a pizza place
blocks.body: If the pizza place baked a fresh pie for every order, customers would wait an hour. So pies are baked before the lunch rush and slices are lined up at the counter. A customer walks in, takes a slice and leaves. The kitchen is the database, and the slices on the counter are the **cache**.

Ryan's homepage shows "the 10 best-selling products". The calculation takes 800ms in the database, and the page is opened 50,000 times a day. The answer barely changes in 10 minutes, yet it is cooked from scratch every time. That adds up to 50,000 x 800ms, about 11 hours of database work a day. Cache the answer for 10 minutes and it is cooked at most 144 times a day, under 2 minutes of work.

blocks.caption: The same answer: calculated in the database vs. fetched from the cache

items.label: Database query
items.tip: It runs a heavy join and group by, recalculating the answer on every request.

items.label: Cache hit
items.tip: The answer stored in advance is handed over straight from memory, with no calculation.

blocks.body: An answer that is needed again and again but rarely changes is a candidate for caching.

items.meaning: The requested answer was found in the cache, so the database wasn't needed.
The answer isn't in the cache, so it had to be fetched from the real source.

aside.body: Stop rebuilding the result of heavy work over and over, so the database is under less pressure and users get answers faster.

check.q: Which kind of answer gains the most from caching?
check.a: One that is requested many times, is heavy to build, and barely changes in a short time, such as the list of the top 10 products.

slides.title: Cache-aside: the app looks, and the app fills
slides.tldr: In cache-aside the app checks the cache first; on a miss it fetches from the database and stores the result itself. It is the most common strategy.

blocks.title: The waiter checks the counter himself
blocks.body: The waiter first looks at the counter for a slice. If there is one, he hands it over at once. If not, he fetches a slice from the kitchen, serves the customer, and leaves one more slice on the counter for the next person. The counter fetches nothing on its own; all the work is the waiter's, which means the app's.

blocks.caption: Cache-aside: on a miss the app fetches from the database and fills the cache

nodes.label: App
nodes.tip: The waiter. Checking the cache, going to the database and filling the cache are all this code's jobs.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.tip: The counter. It only stores things and hands them out on request; it doesn't know how to fetch anything itself.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: The kitchen. Slow, but the correct answer is always here.

edges.label: The app looks in the cache first, using a key
A miss: the cache says it doesn't have it
The app fetches the answer from the database itself
The database returns the answer
The app leaves the answer in the cache with an expiry

blocks.body: Cache-aside: cache first, then the database, then fill the cache.

use: Many reads, few writes: product pages, lists, settings.
The app should keep working off the database even when the cache is down.
avoid: Data that changes every second and must never be shown wrong.

aside.body: The first request is slow (miss), all the later ones are fast (hit).

items: If the cache dies at peak traffic, every request becomes a miss and the database takes the full load at once. A small site survives; a busy one can fall over.

check.q: What does a cache-aside app do when the cache goes down?
check.a: It treats every lookup as a miss and fetches from the database. The app gets slower but stays up, because the truth lives in the database.

slides.title: Cache-aside in Symfony: a single get() call
slides.tldr: Symfony Cache contracts' get(key, callback) looks up, runs the callback on a miss and stores the result; plug in Redis as the backend.

blocks.body: In Symfony you pass the `get()` method of `CacheInterface` a key and a callback. If the key exists, the value comes straight back. If not, the callback runs, its result is stored and returned. You set the expiry with `$item->expiresAfter()`. Without this call, `findTopSelling(10)` would run on every page view, 800ms each time.

marks.tip: Pick a key that tells you what is inside at a glance. The v1 at the end will be useful later.
The callback runs only on a miss. On a hit this code is never touched.
Keep the returned value small and serializable: an array or a DTO, not a Doctrine entity.

blocks.code:
framework:
    cache:
        prefix_seed: 'shop_prod'
        app: cache.adapter.redis
        default_redis_provider: '%env(REDIS_URL)%'

marks.tip: If several apps or environments share one Redis, their keys could collide; the prefix prevents that.
cache.app now writes to Redis. Autowiring CacheInterface gives you this pool.

items: Set maxmemory and an eviction policy (such as allkeys-lru) on Redis, or writes fail once memory is full.
Cache a small DTO or array, not an entity: serializing an entity drags in stale relations and a huge payload.

check.q: When does the callback of a get() call run, and when does it not?
check.a: Only on a miss, meaning the key is missing or has expired. On a hit the stored value comes straight back.

slides.title: Three more strategies for reads and writes
slides.tldr: In read-through, write-through and write-behind the cache itself talks to the database; they differ in when a write reaches the database and where the risk sits.

blocks.body: In cache-aside the waiter does everything. In the other three strategies the person at the counter talks to the kitchen directly. **Read-through**: the counter fetches from the kitchen itself. **Write-through**: the order book and the counter are written at the same time. **Write-behind**: it is noted on the counter first, and copied into the kitchen's book later.

blocks.caption: Who talks to the database in each of the three strategies

columns.title: Read-through
items: On a miss the cache goes to the database itself
The app code stays small
A loader has to be plugged into the cache
columns.tip: A strategy for reads. The app only asks the cache, and on a miss the cache fetches from the source itself.

columns.title: Write-through
items: Writes go to both cache and database
The cache stays fresh
Every write gets slower
columns.tip: The write goes to both places at once and counts as done only when both finish. The cache stays fresh.

columns.title: Write-behind
items: Write to the cache and answer immediately
The database gets it later, in batches
If the cache dies, writes are lost
columns.tip: The write goes to the cache first and to the database later, in batches. Fast, but if the cache dies, unwritten data is lost.

blocks.body: In write-behind, a write that hasn't reached the database lives only in the cache. If the cache dies, it is gone for good.

items: Symfony's get(key, callback) looks like read-through, but it is really cache-aside: the callback is your app's code, not the cache's.
Almost nobody builds write-behind by hand in a PHP app, and certainly not for money or order data.
Where it fits: 5,000 likes a second counted in the cache and saved as one "+5,000" update each second, not 5,000 writes. If the cache dies, that second's likes are lost.

items.meaning: The code that fetches a value from the source on a miss; in read-through it lives inside the cache.

check.q: In which strategy do you risk losing the most data if the cache dies, and why?
check.a: Write-behind. Writes go to the cache first and to the database later, so if the cache dies before they reach the database, those writes are lost.

slides.title: What not to cache, and one terrible mistake
slides.tldr: Caching per-user data under a shared key lets one person see another's data; caching accuracy-critical data like money and stock is risky too.

blocks.body: The most terrible mistake is storing one person's page under a key everyone shares. Put a slice labeled "Ryan's order" on the counter and the next customer will walk off with it. In the code below the key has no user in it, so whoever comes in first has their cart shown to everybody.

marks.tip: The key is just cart. The first user's cart will be shown to everyone for 5 minutes.
Whoever the answer differs for, put their identity in the key.
A short expiry is safer for personal data. Or better still, don't cache such data at all.

blocks.title: Don't cache these
items: Account balances and checkout stock: a wrong value means direct loss.
Data that nobody asks for a second time.
Anything cheap to build, where the cache adds more hassle than it saves.
A query that is slow only because an index is missing, or an N+1 (one extra query per row): fix that first, then see if you still need a cache.
Don't cache a whole page that holds a logged-in user's name or CSRF token under a shared key; it leaks exactly like the cart.

aside.body: If the answer differs per person, that person's identity must be in the key.

check.q: What can happen if the cache key doesn't include the user ID?
check.a: The first user's private data can be seen by everyone after them. That is a direct data leak.

slides.title: Which strategy, and when
slides.tldr: For most Symfony apps cache-aside is enough; use write-through when you need fresh values, and write-behind only for load-absorbing writes where loss is acceptable.

blocks.caption: The four strategies side by side

rows.tip: In cache-aside the app has full control, so it is the simplest and most transparent.
To reduce staleness, use write-through; but every write gets slower.
Write-behind buys speed at the price of a risk of loss.
Never use write-behind for money or order data.
The normal way of using Symfony Cache is cache-aside.

blocks.title: The decision rule
items: When in doubt, cache-aside with a short TTL.
If you need a fresh value right after a write, update or delete the cache entry when you write.
Never use write-behind for data you can't afford to lose.

items.label: How to cure a stale cache

check.q: Which strategy would you start with for an ordinary product page, and why?
check.a: Cache-aside with a short TTL. It is simple, it works with Symfony's get(), and the app still runs off the database when the cache is down.

slides.title: The price changed, the board still shows the old one
slides.tldr: A cached answer is a copy of the real data; when the original changes, the copy doesn't follow, so users see stale data. This problem is called cache invalidation.

blocks.title: The price board at the coffee shop
blocks.body: A board outside the coffee shop says "Latte $4.50". In the morning the price rises to $5.00, but nobody changes the board. A customer reads $4.50, comes to the counter and hears $5.00. The board is the cache, and the owner's price book is the database. When the real price book changes, someone has to change the board too.

In Ryan's app, product prices are cached for 1 hour. A seller drops a price from $50 to $45, and it is saved in the database just fine. But for another 50 minutes, buyers still see $50. Buyers see $50 and many walk away, though the real price is $45.

blocks.caption: Even after the price change, the cache shows the old price

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: The source of truth. The price here is already $45.

actors.label: Cache
actors.tip: Still holding the old answer, because nobody told it to change.

actors.label: Buyer
actors.tip: Gets the answer from the cache and never reaches the database.

messages.label: $50 (old)
messages.tip: It was a cache hit, but the answer is wrong. A fast wrong answer can be worse than a slow correct one.

blocks.body: A cache is a copy. When the original changes, the copy must change too, or be thrown away.

aside.title: The day after a flash sale
aside.body: A site's sale ended at midnight, but its cache expiry was 6 hours. Orders kept arriving at the sale price until 6 a.m., and the company had to honor every one.

items.meaning: Deleting or voiding the cache's old copy when the real data changes.
A copy that has fallen behind the real data.

check.q: The request was a cache hit, yet the buyer saw the wrong price. Is the problem the cache's speed, or something else?
check.a: Not speed. After the real data changed, the cache's copy was never updated, so it is serving a stale answer.

slides.title: TTL: every piece of data gets an expiry
slides.tldr: TTL is the lifetime of a cached answer; when it runs out the entry vanishes. Set it by how stale the data may get, and treat TTL as the last line of defense.

blocks.title: The date on a milk carton
blocks.body: A milk carton has a date on it; once the date passes, nobody drinks it and it is thrown away. TTL (time to live) is that date. But how long it lasts depends on the item: milk 2 days, rice 6 months. So you ask yourself: "How long can this information be out of date without hurting anyone?"

blocks.caption: A sample of choosing a TTL by the kind of data

cells: Does it change even once a year?
rows.tip: For almost unchanging data a long TTL is safe, and the hit rate stays high.

cells: Nobody notices if it is 10 minutes old
rows.tip: The most common case: a heavy calculation where a little staleness is fine.
For data like prices, keep the TTL short and delete the entry the moment it changes.

cells: An approximate display is fine; use the database when buying
rows.tip: Cache for showing, database for deciding.
For some data, a correct answer matters above everything.

blocks.body: TTL is the last line of defense: even if you forget to invalidate, the mistake lasts only until expiry.

items: The question for setting a TTL: "What is the longest this data can be out of date?" That is the upper bound for the TTL.
If you rely on TTL alone, every change shows wrong data until expiry; so add invalidation for important data.
Short TTL means fresher data but more misses. An entry read 100 times a minute costs 1 query a minute at a 1-minute TTL, but about 100 at a 1-second TTL.
Using one TTL for everything, say 1 hour: too long for some data and far too short for others.

check.q: Between a product details page and a "list of countries", which should have the longer TTL, and why?
check.a: The list of countries. It almost never changes, so a long TTL does no harm; product data changes much more often.

slides.title: Cache keys: the right key, and a version
slides.tldr: The key must contain everything that changes the answer: ID, language, page. A version in the key lets you void all entries of an old shape at once.

blocks.body: A key is a locker number: give the wrong number and you get someone else's stuff. Whatever changes the answer goes in the key; whatever doesn't, stays out. And sometimes the shape of every entry changes, say a new field is added. Then you don't delete them one by one: change `v1` in the key to `v2`, and nobody looks up the old ones any more; they die on their own at their TTL.

blocks.caption: What a safe key looks like, and what gives wrong answers

columns.title: Dangerous keys
items: products: no language, page or sort
cart: which user?
user_list: the same for everyone, though it differs by role
columns.tip: Nothing that affects the answer is in the key, so different answers take each other's place.

columns.title: Safe keys
items: products.v2.cat7.page2.sort-price.en
cart.v1.user.42
product.v3.42: when the shape changes, v3 becomes v4
columns.tip: Every different answer has its own key, and old shapes are separated by version.

blocks.body: What changes the answer goes in the key. What doesn't, stays out.

items: Don't use PSR-6's reserved characters `{ } ( ) / \ @ :` in keys. Dots and underscores are safe.
If a key is built from user input, hash it, or you will end up with long or odd keys.
A version bump starts that key family with an empty cache, so the first requests all miss together. Protect hot keys (see the stampede lesson).

use: Bump the version when the shape inside the cache changes (a new field, a rename).
avoid: Bumping the version on every small data change; that is a job for tags or direct deletion.

check.q: You add a new field to the cached product and deploy, so old entries will come back in the wrong shape. What is the simplest fix?
check.a: Bump the key version, for example product.v1.42 to product.v2.42. Nobody looks up the old entries any more, and they die at their TTL.

slides.title: Deleting many entries at once with tags
slides.tldr: One product lives in many cache entries; tag them all, and after a product change a single invalidateTags() call removes every one.

blocks.title: Colored stickers on the board
blocks.body: Latte is written in several places: on the front board, on the menu card, on the offer poster. Each one carries a green "latte" sticker. When the price changes, you can say, "Take down every green sticker." You don't have to remember where latte appeared. A cache tag does exactly this.

marks.tip: You need TagAwareCacheInterface, not the plain CacheInterface; it is the one with invalidateTags().
The list of things this entry depends on. One entry can have several tags.
Call it after the database flush has finished. Called earlier, the old value could get cached again.
The list depends on every product in it, so it carries each product's tag. Without this, changing product 42 would leave the list stale.

blocks.code:
framework:
    cache:
        app: cache.adapter.redis_tag_aware
        default_redis_provider: '%env(REDIS_URL)%'

marks.tip: The tag-aware adapter for Redis. Invalidating by tag takes fewer steps and is faster with it.

items: A category list is tagged with the id of every product in it, so one invalidateTags(['product_42']) removes both the product page and the list.
Shape tag names like keys: product_42, category_7.

items.desc: Delete every entry with a tag, from the console

items: Every tag is stored extra data: a list tagged with 500 products carries 500 tags. Tag short lists, such as one page of 20, and only what you will need to delete.

check.q: When a product changes, you want to delete both its own page and its category list from the cache. How do you do it with tags?
check.a: Give both entries ->tag(['product_42']), then call invalidateTags(['product_42']) once after the product changes.

slides.title: When to delete, and in what order
slides.tldr: Write to the database and commit first, then delete from the cache. The other way around lets one request put the old value back in the cache; so keep a TTL too.

blocks.body: Many people wipe the board first and write the new price in the ledger afterwards. In that gap, an assistant sees the blank board, checks the ledger, finds the old price there, and writes it on the board again. Now the ledger has the new price, the board the old one, and nobody will wipe it again.

blocks.caption: The wrong order: delete from the cache first, write to the database after

actors.label: Writer
actors.tip: The request that changes the price.

actors.label: Reader
actors.tip: Another request that comes to read the price at exactly that moment.

actors.label: Cache
actors.tip: The copy kept for fast reads, which is about to go stale here.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: The source of truth; after the write it holds the new value.

messages.label: Delete the price from the cache
$50 (old)
messages.tip: The writer hasn't written to the database yet, so the old value comes back.
Nobody will delete it again. The wrong price stays until the TTL runs out.

marks.tip: If flush fails, execution never reaches the next line, so the cache is never ahead of the database.
The first request after the delete gets a miss and fetches the new value from the database.

blocks.body: Commit to the database first, then delete from the cache. And always keep a TTL.

aside.body: Truth first, copy after: for writing and for deleting alike.

items: A slow reader can still re-cache the old value: it reads before your commit and stores after your delete. Rare, but real. The TTL cleans it up.
flush() commits only if no outer transaction is open. Inside one (say Messenger's doctrine_transaction middleware), delete after that outer commit.

items.label: The storm of misses after a delete

check.q: If you delete from the cache and then write to the database, how can the old value find its way back into the cache?
check.a: In the gap between the delete and the write, another request gets a miss, reads the old value from the database and stores it in the cache, and nobody deletes it again.

slides.title: The entry expired, and a thousand people rushed in
slides.tldr: When a popular cache entry expires, a thousand requests miss at once and all send the same heavy query to the database; this storm is called a cache stampede.

blocks.title: The train timetable board at the station
blocks.body: Before Thanksgiving, the train times are written on a board at the station, so nobody goes to the ticket counter. Then the board is suddenly wiped. Within a second, a thousand passengers rush to the counter and ask the same thing: "When does it leave?" One clerk can't handle a thousand people. The board is the cache, and the counter is the database.

One heavy query takes 800ms. A thousand of them in the same second is about 800 seconds of database work, roughly 13 minutes squeezed into one second. The database can't keep up, so every other request waits in the queue too.

blocks.caption: Exactly what happens when an entry expires

nodes.label: 1,000 requests
nodes.tip: About a thousand users opening the homepage, all asking for the same key.

nodes.label: App
nodes.tip: Each request checks the cache on its own, and none of them knows the others are doing the same.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.tip: The entry has just died. Every lookup is now a miss.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: Run a heavy query 1,000 times at once and the CPU is gone, and every other request gets stuck too.

edges.label: 1,000 requests ask for the same page in one second
Every request checks the cache first
The entry has just expired, so everyone gets a miss
A thousand requests send the same heavy query to the database
The database gasps and answers slowly

blocks.body: The database survived because the cache was working. When the cache fails all at once, the database fails with it.

aside.title: The hourly slowdown
aside.body: One site's homepage cache entry had a fixed expiry of 1 hour. Once an hour, for a few seconds, the site slowed to a crawl, because when the entry expired, all the requests on the homepage rushed to the database together.

items.meaning: When a popular entry dies and many requests rush to rebuild it at the same time.
Many processes waking up on the same event and pouncing on the same resource.

check.q: Why does the database run the query a thousand times instead of once when a cache entry dies?
check.a: Because each request gets its own miss and nobody knows someone else is doing the same work, so they all run the query on their own at the same moment.

slides.title: One person cooks, the rest wait
slides.tldr: The core of stopping a stampede: for one key only one request rebuilds the value at a time (a lock), and the rest wait or show the stale value.

blocks.title: The one big batch at a wedding buffet
blocks.body: When the pasta runs out at a wedding buffet, one cook starts a fresh batch. The other 100 guests don't each start their own batch on the stove. They wait, or they scrape what is left at the bottom of the tray. The "key to the stove" is the **lock**.

blocks.caption: With a lock, one request goes to the database instead of 1,000

nodes.label: App
nodes.tip: Everyone got a miss. Now the question is: who does the calculation?

nodes.label: Lock
nodes.tip: A separate lock per key. Whoever gets it is the cook; the rest don't.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: Now one heavy query arrives, not a thousand.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.tip: The cook puts the finished value here; after that everyone gets a hit.

edges.label: After a miss everyone asks for the lock, and only one gets it
Only the one who got the lock runs the heavy query
The result is stored in the cache
The others wait, or take the stale value and then get the new one

blocks.title: The two paths for those who didn't get the lock
items: Wait briefly: check the cache again after 200ms. By then the cook has probably finished.
Stale value: show the previous (slightly old) value straight away. No waiting at all.

blocks.body: For one key, only one request calculates at a time. The rest wait or take the stale value.

aside.body: Reducing a thousand identical heavy jobs to a single job. It is also called request coalescing.

check.q: What can the requests that didn't get the lock do, so the database isn't put under extra load?
check.a: They can wait briefly and check the cache again, or immediately show the stale (old) value.

slides.title: Spread out the expiry: jitter and early expiration
slides.tldr: Adding a random few seconds to the expiry (jitter) stops many entries dying together; and Symfony's beta parameter lets one request rebuild the value slightly before it expires.

blocks.body: Entries that are all set at the same moment die at the same moment. So add a little random time (**jitter**) to the expiry. Go one step further: the `beta` parameter of Symfony's `get()` asks, shortly before expiry and with a small probability, for some request to rebuild the value ahead of time. The closer the expiry, the higher the probability. So usually somebody has already rebuilt it, and no storm rises at the moment of expiry.

marks.tip: Entries built at the same moment now die at different times: 1,000 entries spread over 2 minutes expire about 8 a second, not 1,000 at once.
1.0 is the default. A higher value starts trying earlier, but costs more extra cooking.

blocks.caption: Four protections: what each one stops

cells: Some entries die a little early
rows.tip: Almost free, and worth adding every time.
Symfony does this itself; no code needed.

cells: The others wait or get a stale value
rows.tip: Symfony's LockRegistry works within one server; across several servers you add your own lock.

cells: Show stale, rebuild behind the scenes
A slightly old value for a while
rows.tip: The next slide has the code for this.

items: Symfony's own LockRegistry stops several simultaneous calculations of one key on a single server. With many servers each keeps its own lock, so you need a shared lock there.
Making the jitter range 10 to 20 percent of the base TTL is a good start.

check.q: Jitter and beta both play with the expiry. What is the difference in what they do?
check.a: Jitter spreads the expiry of many entries over different moments, so they don't all die together. Beta makes someone rebuild a single entry before its expiry arrives.

slides.title: Show the stale one, build the new one behind
slides.tldr: Give an entry a soft expiry and a hard expiry; once the soft one passes, one request takes a lock and rebuilds, while the rest get the old value.

blocks.body: With this technique the user never waits. An entry has two times: **soft** (5 minutes, after which it is "nearly stale") and **hard** (1 hour, after which the cache itself deletes it). Once the soft time passes, the first request to get the lock builds the new value, while everyone else immediately gets the old one.

marks.tip: If soft time remains, return straight away. Most requests end right here.
By default acquire() doesn't wait; it returns true or false at once. So nobody gets stuck.
beta: INF means "rebuild now", even though the cache entry hasn't expired.
Always release the lock in finally. If you don't, nobody can refresh for up to 30 seconds (the lock's TTL) and users keep getting the old value.

blocks.body: Giving the user a 5-minute-old answer is often better than making them sit through 800ms.

use: Homepages, lists, reports: places where a value a few minutes old is fine.
avoid: Accuracy-critical data such as money or stock.

items: The hard TTL is only a safety net: a busy key is refreshed at the soft time and never reaches it. A quiet key can, and the next requests then miss together.
In bigger systems, don't do the refresh inside the request; send a Messenger message and let a worker do it, so no user is ever slowed.

check.q: If 100 requests arrive together after the soft expiry has passed, how many will build the new value, and what do the rest get?
check.a: Just one, the request that gets the lock. The other 99 don't get the lock and immediately receive the old (nearly stale) value.

slides.title: The lock itself can become a new danger
slides.tldr: A lock without an expiry, or waiting forever, leaves everyone stuck if the holder dies and runs the PHP workers out; give the lock a TTL and put a limit on waiting.

blocks.body:
If the cook takes the key to the stove and goes home, the other 100 people wait forever. The same happens in code: the request holding the lock crashes, and the rest sit in `acquire(true)`. Every waiting request holds on to a PHP worker, so soon the workers run out and the whole site stops.

A typical PHP server has maybe 20 workers (processes that each handle one request at a time). Twenty waiting requests are enough to freeze it.

marks.tip: The default lock TTL is 300 seconds. If the holder crashes, nobody can get in for 5 minutes.
true means blocking. Every waiting request holds a worker.
If an exception is thrown, release() never runs. Without try/finally, the lock hangs.
A short TTL: even if the holder dies, the lock frees itself after 30 seconds. If the job needs longer, you have to call refresh().
Non-blocking: if you don't get it, take the alternative path straight away.
A guarantee that the lock is released, whatever happens.

items: Don't make the waiters simply fail; keep a fallback, such as the stale value, or a short wait and then calculating it themselves.
Make the lock TTL a bit longer than the longest the calculation can take, or the lock will let go while the work is still running.

aside.body: A lock without a TTL and a release without try/finally: both are homes of the hanging lock.

check.q: If the request holding the lock crashes, what happens if the lock has a TTL, and what would happen if it didn't?
check.a: With a TTL, the lock frees itself when it expires and the others carry on. Without one (or with a very long one), everyone sits waiting and the PHP workers run out.

slides.title: Downloading the same file every time
slides.tldr: Without Cache-Control, the browser and the CDN don't know what to keep, so the same JS, images and API answers come from the origin server on every visit. HTTP caching stops this waste.

blocks.title: The newspaper and the neighborhood newsstand
blocks.body: Newspapers are printed at the press. If every reader had to go to the press every day, nobody would get a paper. So the neighborhood newsstand brings in many copies at once, and readers take theirs home and leave it on the table. The press is your server, the newsstand is the **CDN**, and the copy on the table is the browser's cache.

On Ryan's site, `app.js` is 2.4MB and changes once a week. Yet every page load makes the browser download it again. At 50,000 visits a day, that is 120GB of bandwidth. The server keeps handing out the same file and users keep waiting.

blocks.caption: The same app.js in three situations: KB downloaded per visit

items.label: No rules
items.tip: The browser doesn't know what to do, so it downloads the whole file every time.

items.label: ETag + 304
items.tip: The browser asks "has it changed?"; the server answers "no" with headers alone. No body is downloaded.

items.label: Within max-age
items.tip: The browser asks the server nothing and simply uses its own copy.

blocks.body: The fastest and cheapest request is the one that never reaches the server.

items.meaning: A network of servers spread around the world that serve copies of your files from close to the user.
The real server, where the CDN fetches a file from the first time.

aside.body: Not fetching the same copy from the server again and again, so pages open faster and server costs fall.

check.q: Between a file within its max-age and a file validated with an ETag, which one sends no request to the server at all?
check.a: The file within its max-age. The browser uses its own copy directly. With an ETag, it still sends a small request to ask.

slides.title: Cache-Control: who keeps it, and for how long
slides.tldr: The Cache-Control header says who (the browser or the CDN) may keep an answer and for how long: max-age, s-maxage, public, private, no-cache, no-store, stale-while-revalidate.

blocks.body: Along with the answer, the server sends an instruction: Cache-Control. In newsstand language: "Keep this paper at home, for 1 day", "Don't keep this at the newsstand, only the reader may", "Don't keep this anywhere". The most common mistake is mixing up `no-cache` and `no-store`.

blocks.caption: The most useful Cache-Control directives

cells: The browser may use it for 600 seconds without asking the server
rows.tip: While the lifetime lasts, the request never reaches the server.

cells: A separate lifetime for shared caches (the CDN) only
rows.tip: Use this to give the browser a short lifetime and the CDN a long one.

cells: public: the CDN may keep it too. private: only the user's browser
rows.tip: For personal answers, always use private (or no-store).

cells: You may keep it, but check with the server every time
rows.tip: The name misleads: it doesn't mean "don't keep it", it means "don't use it without asking".
For sensitive answers such as bank details or tokens.

cells: After expiry, serve the old copy for 60 more seconds while fetching a new one
rows.tip: The user doesn't wait; the cache refreshes itself in the background.

blocks.body: no-cache means "don't use it without asking". If you want nothing kept, use no-store.

aside.body: private = only your own table, public = the newsstand may keep it too.

items: Never put public on any answer for a logged-in user.
stale-while-revalidate isn't only for HTTP; the same idea applies to a cache inside your server.

check.q: Which Cache-Control would you put on the JSON answer for a user's own profile, public or private?
check.a: private (and no-store if it is sensitive). With public, a CDN could show one user's profile to other people.

slides.title: ETag: has it changed? No, so no download
slides.tldr: An ETag is the fingerprint of an answer. The browser sends it back in If-None-Match; if it matches, the server replies 304 with no body and the browser uses its own copy.

blocks.title: The issue number of a newspaper
blocks.body: A reader goes to the newsstand and says, "I have issue number 741. Is that the latest?" The owner checks and says, "Yes, keep it." The reader doesn't need a new paper. The issue number is the ETag, and "Yes, keep it" is the 304.

blocks.caption: A conditional request with an ETag

actors.label: Browser
actors.tip: Has kept the earlier answer and its ETag.

actors.label: Server
actors.tip: Compares fingerprints and sends the body only if needed.

messages.label: 200 + ETag: "v7a1" + body
messages.tip: The first time, the whole answer goes out along with its fingerprint.

messages.note: Stores the answer and the ETag

messages.label: GET + If-None-Match: "v7a1"
messages.tip: The browser is saying "I have v7a1, has it changed?"

messages.label: 304 Not Modified (no body)
messages.tip: The fingerprint matches. The server sends only headers, a few hundred bytes.

messages.label: If-None-Match again, after the product changed
200 + new ETag: "v7b2" + body
messages.tip: The fingerprint doesn't match, so the whole new answer goes out.

blocks.body: An ETag saves the cost of the body, not the cost of the request. To save the request itself, use max-age.

items.meaning: A request with a condition: "send it only if it has changed" (If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since).
Starts with W/"..."; it is enough for the meaning to be the same, even if it isn't byte-for-byte identical.

items: Last-Modified and If-Modified-Since do the same job with dates. ETag is more reliable, because it catches changes within a second too.

check.q: When the ETag matches, what does the server send, and what does that save?
check.a: 304 Not Modified, with no body. It saves downloading the body, and if the ETag can be checked cheaply, it saves the work of building the body too.

slides.title: Headers and 304 in Symfony
slides.tldr: Use the #[Cache] attribute to set max-age, public and stale-while-revalidate; build an ETag and call response->isNotModified() to return 304 before any heavy work.

blocks.body: In Symfony, the `Response` object builds the cache headers. For an ordinary lifetime, the `#[Cache]` attribute is enough. For ETags the trick is to build the ETag from something cheap to get, such as `updatedAt`. That way you can compare and return a 304 before building the heavy JSON.

marks.tip: The browser keeps it for 1 minute and the CDN for 10. Even after expiry, a copy up to 2 minutes old is still allowed.
The ETag is built from the ID and the time of the last change. No need to build the body.
isNotModified() compares the request's If-None-Match, and if it matches, sets the 304 for you.
A personal answer: saying private is the shortest form of protection.
If you don't want even the browser to store it, no-store.

items: When a session is used, Symfony makes the response private by itself; still, state it explicitly on a personal API.
Price: with s-maxage=600 a changed product can look old for up to 10 minutes; for prices and stock use short lifetimes or purge.
Can an answer change in many ways? Put every ingredient (ID, updatedAt, language) into the ETag.

check.q: Why is the ETag built from the ID and updatedAt, and not from a hash of the whole JSON?
check.a: To hash the JSON you must build the whole JSON first, which wipes out the gain from a 304. updatedAt is cheap to get, so you can compare and return before the heavy work.

slides.title: CDN, cache keys and cache busting
slides.tldr: A CDN builds its cache key from the URL (and any Vary headers); a hash in the file name plus a one-year immutable lifetime means a new deploy bypasses the old file's cache by itself.

blocks.caption: How a CDN serves the same file to many people

nodes.label: User
nodes.tip: Sends the request to a nearby CDN server.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.tip: Builds a cache key from the URL and the Vary headers, then looks up a copy with that key.

nodes.label: Origin server
nodes.tip: Called only on a miss. It tells the CDN how long to keep the file, using Cache-Control.

edges.label: The user asks the nearby CDN for the file
The CDN doesn't have it (miss), so it goes to the origin
The server sends the file and Cache-Control
The CDN keeps a copy and gives the file to the user
When the next person asks for the same file, the CDN serves it directly (hit)

blocks.body: A CDN's cache key is usually the URL, so `/app.js?v=1` and `/app.js?v=2` are different keys. With `Vary: Accept-Language` it keeps a separate copy per language. Now Ryan gives `/assets/app.js` a one-year lifetime and deploys a fix on Friday under the same name. Every browser thinks its copy is fresh for 360 more days, so it never asks, and users keep running the buggy file. **Cache busting** fixes this: put a hash of the contents in the name (`app-3f9a1c.js`).

blocks.caption: The same Friday deploy, with and without a hash in the name

columns.title: Same name, 1-year lifetime
items: Monday: browsers store /assets/app.js for a year
Friday: the fixed file is deployed under the same URL
Browsers think their copy is fresh, so no request is sent
Result: old, buggy JS for up to a year
columns.tip: The URL is the cache key. Same URL means the browser sees nothing new.

columns.title: Hashed name, 1-year lifetime
items: Monday: browsers store app-3f9a1c.js for a year
Friday: the fix is app-9b2e7d.js, and the HTML now links to it
The short-lived HTML is re-fetched and shows the new name
Result: the new file on the next page view
columns.tip: The name changes with the contents, so the URL (and cache key) changes too.

marks.tip: immutable says this file will never change, so don't ask even on a reload.
If you give HTML a long lifetime, users will keep seeing links to the old files even after a new deploy.

blocks.body: Put a hash in the file name and give it a year. Always keep HTML on a short lifetime.

items: Symfony AssetMapper, Webpack Encore and Vite all add a hash to file names in production. You don't have to do it yourself.
Keep the previous hashed files on the server for a while after a deploy; a page opened just before it may still ask for them.
If a file gets stuck in the CDN by mistake and it is urgent, delete it with the CDN's purge/invalidate feature.

use: Files built from your own code (JS, CSS, images), where a build tool can hash the name.
avoid: URLs that must stay fixed, like robots.txt or a script partners embed: use a short max-age plus an ETag.

items: `Vary: Cookie`, or a different query string on every request, gives every request its own key, and the hit rate drops to almost zero.

check.q: If you deploy new code to an app.js with a one-year lifetime, how will users get the new file?
check.a: The new file's name gets a new hash (app-9b2e7d.js), and the HTML links to that new name. A new URL means a new cache key, so the old copy never comes into it.

slides.title: The wrong public: one person's page for everyone
slides.tldr: Putting public or s-maxage on a personal or cookie-dependent answer lets the CDN serve one user's page to others; that is a direct data leak.

blocks.body: At the neighborhood newsstand, if a paper brought in for Ryan, with his name on it, is put out "for everyone", Kevin will walk away with it. In the code below, the dashboard has `public` and `smaxage`. The CDN will show the first user's dashboard to everybody for 10 minutes.

marks.tip: public + smaxage = the CDN keeps a copy for 10 minutes, for whoever asks the same URL.
The answer depends on getUser(), yet the cache key has no user in it.
private: only the user's own browser may keep it. The CDN won't.

blocks.title: Three questions before you make something public
items: Is the answer exactly the same for every user?
Does the request carry a cookie or Authorization header that changes the answer?
If something like language or country changes the answer, is there a Vary header?
Resist the temptation to make everything public to raise the CDN hit rate; one wrong public header is one data leak.
Testing only in the app won't catch this mistake; check the headers and the answer from in front of the CDN.

aside.body: A personal answer = private (or no-store). public means "everyone gets the same thing".

check.q: What is the risk of putting Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=600 on an API answer that comes with an Authorization header?
check.a: The CDN stores the answer by URL and may give it to another user, so one person's private data is seen by someone else.
